issues.legal_issue: A statutory restriction on dismantling a factory or removing its machinery does not bar delivery of possession of the factory premises in execution of a decree.
material_facts: The decree-holder sought execution of a decree for possession of premises used as a factory.
Machinery was installed or stored in the premises, and its removal required prior written permission from the relevant government authority.
The execution sought delivery of possession; the court’s order for possession did not itself require the factory to be dismantled or the machinery to be removed.
issues.conclusion: The Act did not bar delivery of possession of the premises in execution of the decree.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(1) of the East Punjab Factories (Control of Dismantling) Act, 1948 prohibited dismantling a factory or removing specified spare parts without written permission. The Act made no reference to a decree for possession, and an executing court’s order transferring possession did not itself constitute dismantling or removal. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.execution_of_possession_decree: The proceeding is execution of a decree that directs delivery of possession of premises.
predicates.execution_order_only_transfers_possessio: The executing court’s order transfers possession without itself requiring the factory machinery to be removed.
predicates.execution_order_does_not_require_dismant: The order being executed does not direct the factory to be dismantled or machinery to be removed.

issues.definition: When a possession decree is being executed by transferring possession without ordering dismantling or removal, the dismantling restriction does not bar delivery of possession.

issues.legal_issue: Earlier execution proceedings do not make the executability of a possession decree res judicata when the earlier orders did not finally decide that issue.
material_facts: The decree-holder made earlier applications to execute a decree for possession of factory premises.
The first execution proceedings did not result in a final order declaring the decree inexecutable.
A later High Court order expressly stated that the record did not permit a decision on whether execution would defeat the statutory restriction and remanded the matter for a fresh decision.
The proceedings following the remand led to the order under appeal.
issues.conclusion: The earlier execution proceedings did not make the question of executability res judicata.
issues.legal_principle: Res judicata did not apply because there had been no final adjudication of the decree’s executability in the earlier execution proceedings. In particular, an order expressly stating that the issue could not be decided on the record and remanding it for a fresh decision was not a final order. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: execution_of_possession_decree and earlier_execution_proceedings_exist and no_final_order_decided_executability and remand_order_left_executability_undecided

predicates.execution_of_possession_decree: The proceeding concerns execution of a decree directing delivery of possession.
predicates.earlier_execution_proceedings_exist: The parties previously litigated execution of the same possession decree.
predicates.no_final_order_decided_executability: No final order in the earlier proceedings decided whether the decree could be executed.
predicates.remand_order_left_executability_undecide: A remand order stated that the record did not permit a decision on executability and directed the issue to be decided afresh.

issues.definition: When earlier execution proceedings produced no final decision on executability and a remand left that issue open, those proceedings do not bar the issue as res judicata.
